opus-5.5.text:
I think when I was in the Yao Class, my feelings about theoretical computer science were actually quite mixed, and they changed over time.

At the beginning, I was really drawn to it. Theory has this beauty: you define a problem very cleanly, you prove something, and it's true forever. For a young student that's very attractive. You feel like you're touching something fundamental. The Yao Class culture also emphasized that a lot. Many of the best students went into theory, and there was a sense that this was the "hard" and "pure" thing to do.

But gradually I started asking myself: what is the practical significance of this? Theory is very good at answering questions once the questions are well-defined. But in the real world, the most important part is often figuring out what the right question is. Many theoretical results are elegant, but the connection to how systems are actually built, or how intelligence actually works, can be quite far. Sometimes you prove a bound, and it's beautiful, but it doesn't really change what anyone does.

So I felt that theory trained a certain way of thinking: rigor, abstraction, breaking a problem into its essential structure. That's extremely valuable, and I still use it. When I think about agents or language models, I try to ask what the essential abstraction is, what the minimal formulation looks like. That habit comes from theory training.

But I also realized I personally wanted to work on something where the problem itself is still being defined, where it's messy and empirical and moving very fast. AI, especially around 2018, 2019, felt like that. It was less clear what the right formalism was, and that's exactly what made it exciting to me. In a way, the most interesting theory is often done after a field matures, and I was more excited about being there when it's still forming.

So I wouldn't say theory is impractical. I'd say its significance is more about shaping how you think, rather than directly giving you the answer to the problems that matter most right now.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes theory as elegant and sometimes disconnected from practice, but does not say Shunyu Yao thought the important problems in theoretical computer science might already have been solved.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention graph algorithms, polynomial exponents, or the practical significance of small complexity improvements.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: To be honest, when I was in Yao Class, I didn't think much about practical significance at all. Yao Class is very theory-heavy. The core courses are things like computational complexity, algorithms, cryptography, information theory. You spend most of your time proving things. And at the time, the culture was that theory is the beautiful part of computer science, and the practical stuff is almost like engineering details that someone else can handle.

I actually enjoyed that. There's a certain purity to it. You take a problem, you abstract it into a clean mathematical object, and you ask what is fundamentally possible. Can this be solved in polynomial time? What's the lower bound? That training really shapes how you think.

But I'll also say I had a bit of a crisis around my junior or senior year. I started asking myself, what am I actually going to do with this? I was reasonably good at theory, but I wasn't the kind of person who could spend ten years on one open problem. And I realized a lot of the deepest theory results, while intellectually gorgeous, had a pretty indirect path to changing anything in the real world.

Looking back, what I'd say is that Yao Class gave me something more valuable than any specific theorem. It gave me a way of thinking. When I later moved into AI, especially into agents and language models, I found myself constantly doing the same thing: trying to find the right abstraction. What is the right way to define the problem? What is the environment, what is the action space, what does it mean to succeed? That is fundamentally a theory mindset, even if there are no proofs involved.

So my answer evolved. In school, I thought theory was valuable because it was elegant. Now I think theory is valuable because it teaches you to ask what the real problem is before you start solving it. In AI right now, a lot of people are very good at solving, and surprisingly few people are good at defining. The defining part is where I feel the Yao Class training actually pays off.

r001.rationale: The response describes a later crisis about applying theory, but never says he suspected the important theoretical problems had already been solved.

astra-6.text:
在姚班读书的时候，我觉得理论计算机科学最重要的价值，是教你怎么把一个问题想清楚：它的假设是什么，难点在哪里，什么情况下能解决，什么情况下根本不可能解决。这种训练未必马上对应一个产品，但它会影响你后来做研究的方式。

当然，理论上的重要性和实际中的重要性也不完全一样。一个算法在渐近复杂度上更好，不代表它在现实的数据规模和计算条件下就更好用。反过来，一个方法实践中很有效，我们也可能还没有特别完整的理论解释。

所以我会把理论看成一种很有价值的基础，但不是判断问题价值的唯一标准。除了问一个问题在数学上是不是漂亮，也要问：现实中是不是真的有人需要解决它？

r001.rationale: The candidate describes theory as a way to clarify assumptions, difficulty, and solvability, but does not say he suspected the important theoretical problems were already solved.

r002.rationale: The candidate notes that better asymptotic complexity does not necessarily improve practical performance, but does not specifically convey that small reductions in a graph algorithm’s polynomial exponent had little practical significance.

sol-6.1.text:
At the time, I was drawn to the elegance of theoretical computer science: you could define a problem precisely and reason rigorously about what was possible. But I also wondered how much those results would matter in practice. A theoretical guarantee doesn’t automatically tell you whether something will work well in the real world.

I think the practical value is partly in the habits it develops—identifying assumptions, choosing the right abstraction, and understanding the limits of an approach. At the same time, you have to be willing to question whether your abstraction captures the problem you actually care about. For me, that tension between rigorous reasoning and practical usefulness was an important part of studying in the Yao Class.
